title: Sewn-through plywood album
subtitle: Japanese stab-style sewing through drilled wooden boards
excerpt: A sewn-through plywood album uses thin plywood instead of bookbinding board for the covers, drilled at the sewing stations. The wood takes the stab-stitch pattern well and produces a cover that ages to a warm patina. This version uses a basic yotsume (four-hole) pattern.
sourceNotes: The Japanese stab-binding tradition (yotsume toji) is documented in pre-1928 Japanese bookbinding manuals held in the Diet Library, Tokyo, and referenced in Western conservation literature. The application to drilled wooden boards is a modern workshop extension of the same sewing pattern.

glossaryTerms.definition: The basic Japanese stab-binding stitch using four holes. The thread runs a continuous pattern looping over the spine edge and through each hole in a set sequence.

A binding method where the needle passes through the entire stack of pages and covers from front to back, stitching through all layers in a single set of holes rather than sewing signatures separately.

content.text: A sewn-through plywood album is a
whose covers are 3 to 4 mm plywood drilled at each

sewing station. The thread loops between the holes in the standard four-hole pattern. A 3 mm HSS drill bit in a hand drill or cordless driver makes the holes cleanly. The text block does not open flat (stab bindings never do), so this format suits a photo album, a printed sketchbook, or a display book rather than a working journal.

attrs.heading: Drilling the boards
attrs.body: Clamp or tape the plywood to a scrap block before drilling so the bit does not pull through and splinter the underside. Drill at slow speed with light pressure.

items.name: Plywood, 3-4 mm birch, two pieces
items.notes: Cut to the final cover size. Birch ply is fine-grained and sands smooth. Mark and drill sewing stations 8 mm from the spine edge, 4 holes, evenly spaced vertically.

items.name: 3 mm HSS drill bit + hand drill or cordless driver
items.notes: Clamp a scrap of wood behind the plywood while drilling to prevent exit-side splintering.

items.name: Text block pages
items.notes: Watercolour paper, cartridge, or photo paper cut to match the boards. Pierce all layers with the bookbinding awl at the same station marks as the plywood. The awl works on paper but not on plywood (use the drill for the boards only).

items.name: Waxed linen thread, 4-cord
items.notes: About five times the height of the book. The yotsume pattern is thread-intensive.

items.name: Sandpaper, 180 grit
items.notes: For sanding the plywood edges smooth before sewing. Round the corners slightly so the thread does not cut against a sharp edge.

content.text: Prepare the covers and text block

Sand both plywood covers with 180-grit sandpaper, rounding the corners and edges slightly. Mark the four sewing stations on the spine edge: 10 mm from head, 10 mm from tail, and two evenly spaced between (approximately 40 mm apart on a 210 mm cover). Clamp the cover to a scrap block and drill all four stations with the 3 mm bit. Mark matching stations on the text block pages and pierce with the bookbinding awl while the stack is clamped in a book press or under heavy weights.
Assemble and sew the yotsume pattern

Stack the text block between the two covers, aligning the sewing stations. Clip or tape the stack at the foredge to hold it square while sewing. Thread the needle with the waxed linen. Begin at hole 1 (the second from the tail): enter from the back cover to the front. Loop over the spine edge and back through the same hole. Run to hole 2 (tail hole), exit through the back, loop over the tail edge and spine, and return through hole 2. Continue in the
through all four holes, looping over the spine between each. Tie off at the starting hole with two half-hitches.

Sand the cover again lightly with 240-grit paper to remove any marks from handling. Apply a light coat of beeswax or a wood oil (linseed or tung) to the plywood with a clean cloth and buff to a soft finish. The thread at the sewing stations should sit neatly and not pull through the wood. If a station splinters, fill the drill hole with a small wooden plug and re-drill in a slightly different position.

The same construction works with the asanoha (hemp-leaf) or kikko (tortoiseshell) stitch patterns at five and six stations respectively. The plywood can be laser-engraved with a design before drilling, or painted before assembly.
